# Diagnosing Rough Idle on the Toyota 1KR-FE Engine

A rough idle on a 2005 Toyota Vitz equipped with the 1KR-FE engine, particularly when the vehicle is stationary in Park or Neutral, points to an imbalance in the air-fuel mixture or mechanical stability. The fact that the issue worsens when the A/C is engaged provides a critical diagnostic clue: the engine control unit (ECU) is being asked to maintain idle speed under increased load, and it may be struggling to compensate. Since there are no Check Engine lights, we can rule out catastrophic failures like a misfire severe enough to trigger codes P0300âP0304, but this does not mean the drivability issue is benign.

The 1KR-FE is a DOHC 16-valve engine known for its efficiency, but it relies heavily on precise vacuum signals and airflow management to stabilize idle. When the A/C compressor engages, it introduces a sudden drop in manifold pressure. The ECU expects this load change and adjusts the throttle plate position via the Idle Air Control (IAC) valve or the electronic throttle body (ETB). If the IAC valve is stuck due to carbon buildupâa common issue on 15-year-old vehiclesâthe throttle cannot open enough to maintain the target RPM, resulting in that shaking vibration.

However, assuming regular servicing with 98RON fuel makes fuel quality a lower probability cause, though not impossible. The most likely culprit involves the variable intake manifold system or the Electronic Throttle Body itself. On many Gen-2 Vitz models, the throttle body is an integral part of the ECU loop rather than a simple mechanical cable. If the stepper motor inside the ETB is failing or if the throttle plate is hanging slightly open/closed due to wear, the idle will fluctuate whenever the load changes.

To address this without immediately replacing expensive components, start with the vacuum side of the equation. The 1KR-FE utilizes a variable length intake manifold (VIM) system to optimize torque at different RPMs. A failing VIM actuator motor can cause erratic air distribution between cylinders, leading to roughness even when the engine is warmed up. Inspect all vacuum hoses connected to the brake booster, PCV valve, and EGR solenoid. A cracked hose or a leaking seal around the intake manifold gaskets will allow unmetered air to enter the system, throwing off the fuel calculation.

If visual inspection yields no leaks, cleaning the throttle body and IAC valve is the next logical step. Use a specific throttle body cleaner that does not leave residue; harsh solvents can damage the internal stepper motor gears. After cleaning, you must perform an idle relearn procedure. On the 1KR-FE, simply turning the key off and on is often insufficient. The ECU needs to recalibrate the learned values for idle speed and throttle position.

One specific technique involves disconnecting the battery negative terminal for about 30 seconds after cleaning the throttle body, then reconnecting it. Start the engine and let it reach operating temperature without touching the accelerator pedal. Allow the engine to idle until the cooling fan cycles at least once; this ensures the ECU has logged the new idle characteristics under high-load conditions.

If the rough idle persists specifically when the A/C is on, check the A/C compressor clutch engagement point for excessive play or a failing internal valve that creates a vacuum leak during cycling. Sometimes, a worn serpentine belt causing slippage at the idler pulley can also induce vibration that mimics an engine misfire.

Finally, consider the possibility of a software calibration issue. While less common than hardware faults, some 2005 models have had recalls or TSBs regarding idle control logic. If mechanical cleaning and inspection do not resolve the load-dependent roughness, flashing the ECU to the latest factory calibration via an OBD-II scanner might be necessary. This ensures the fuel maps and idle target RPMs match the specific hardware configuration of your vehicle.
